Report by Richard Cowan 

(MarijuanaNews note: I wish it were possible for all of the victims of lawless law enforcement to fight back the way that Eric Sage has done. In the real world too many people lack the resources to do so, and all too often there is real danger in standing up for our rights -- meaning everyone’s rights.) 

Report by Bob Newland

On August 7, 2007, Eric Sage was accused of a crime –possession of drug paraphernalia-- for which there was no evidence. That was a crime in itself, committed by South Dakota Highway Patrolman Dave Trautman. 

AssistantPenningtonCountyState’s Attorney Gina Nelson then committed another crime by charging Sage with a different crime for which there was no evidence. 

On April 14, 2008, the Disciplinary Board of the South Dakota State Bar “admonished” Ms. Nelson. 

Eric Sage has initiated an action that might result in a huge expense to the taxpayers of the countyMs. Nelson serves. 

The early chapters of this story have been recounted in the Drug War Chronicles. 

And at Stupid Nark Tricks from South Dakota for the Important and Outrageous Cases File. Kafka Would Understand. Bob Newland Reports. 

And 

at Lawless Law Enforcement “Mugs” Innocent Man. Prosecutorial Abuse in South Dakota. Follow Up On “Stupid Nark Tricks” Bob Newland Reports 

You need to read the testimony offered in the Disciplinary Board hearing. Ms. Nelson’s defense of her actions is a study in arrogance and ignorance. I know that comes as no surprise to those on this list, but to see it offered as rationale in a written document is sobering. 

At the link above, you’ll be able to read all the documents than led to the Disc. Cmmte.’s decision. Then you can consider this: 

What would happen to you if you said your neighbor stole your lawnmower when you had no reason to do say that? What would happen to you if you then called him and threatened him physically, trying to make him pay you $500.00 and make a public admission to stealing the lawnmower you had no reason think he took? What should happen to you? 

An assistant state’s attorney in South Dakota recently was admonished by the State Bar Association for similar actions. Admonished.

Eric Sage was stopped by So. Dak. Highway Patrolman Dave Trautman as he rode his motorcycle towards his Sydney, Nebr. , home last August 7. Sage, 31, was leaving after camping a couple of nights at the Sturgis Rally. His friends, Jorge, Barb and Kalie were in Sage’s pickup, which also stopped when Eric was pulled over. 

During the ensuing events, Trautman found a pipe normally associated with cannabis ingestion, along with an apparently empty-but-dusty-inside baggie. They were in Barb’s purse; she said they were hers. He charged all four people with “possession of paraphernalia,” then said, “Drive carefully,” and let them go. 

A couple of the people in the pickup paid up. Jorge may or may not. Eric went to court. He asked AssistantPenningtonCountyState’s Attorney Gina Nelson to look at the HP dash-cam video to verify that he was not even in the same vehicle as the pipe. 

Nelson chose instead to replace Eric’s paraphernalia charge with “ingestion of a substance other than alcohol for the purpose of intoxication.” Eric suggested again that she look at the video. Nelson scheduled a preliminary hearing (to assure a judge that there was, indeed, sufficient evidence to go to trial on) for Nov. 21, 2008. Eric had already made the 500-mile round-trip from Sydney twice.

 

Eric retained a lawyer, Rena Hymans, of Sturgis. Rena called Gina on several successive days between Nov. 16 and Nov. 21, asking if she were really going to have a preliminary hearing with the evidence she had. She had to leave a message each time, which she did. Nelson didn’t return any of the call. When Eric arrived at the courthouse on Nov. 21, he  and Rena were greeted with a note at the Clerk of Courts counter; “Case dismissed on Nov. 16.” 

By this time, Eric had expended over $4000.00 and all of his patience. He filed a complaint with the Disciplinary Committee of the State Bar of South Dakota, charging that Ms. Nelson had violated several canons of its Code of Professional Conduct. Among them were these two: 

Rule 3.8. Special Responsibilities of a Prosecutor. 

The prosecutor in a criminal case shall: 

(a) refrain from prosecuting a charge that the prosecutor knows is not supported by probable cause; and 

Rule 4.4. Respect for Rights of Third Persons. 

(a) In representing a client, a lawyer shall not use means that have no substantial purpose other than to embarrass, delay, or burden a third person, or use methods of obtaining evidence that violate the legal rights of such a person. 

On April 16, Sage received a letter from the Disciplinary Board of the So. Dak. State Bar, informing him that it had “concluded that Ms. Nelson violated Rules 3.8 and 4.4 in this case. The Board has imposed disciplinary action in the form of an admonition.”

If Eric had committed Ms. Nelson’s crimes, it’s likely he’d be treated a bit more severely. He was, after all, threatened with prison and a fine for a considerably less potentially harmful offense. 

Sage will now pursue restitution for his financial damages.
